{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}
[[File:Uniform tree.svg|thumb|300px|Section of the uniform tree for graph <math>G</math>]]
In mathematics, a '''uniform tree''' is a locally finite [[tree (graph theory)|tree]] which is the [[universal cover]] of a [[finite graph]]. Equivalently, the full [[automorphism group]] <math>G=Aut(X)</math> of the tree, which is a [[locally compact topological group]], is [[unimodular group|unimodular]] and <math>G/X</math> is finite. Also equivalent is the existence of a uniform [[tree lattice|X-lattice]] in <math>G</math>.

For a graph <math>G</math> which contains no [[cycle (graph theory)|cycles]], <math>G</math> is its own uniform tree. If <math>G</math> contains at least 1 cycle, its uniform tree is an infinite tree.

'''Leighton's Graph Covering Theorem''' states that any two finite graphs that share a common covering must also share a common finite covering. Walter D. Neumann expanded on this in 2011, proving any two graphs that have a common covering necessarily have the same universal covering. This means that every uniform tree corresponds to a unique family of finite graphs.
